## Agent conventions (canons)

These apply to every coding agent working in this repository (Codex, Claude Code, Cursor, Copilot and others). Each item states the outcome it wants and why; any concrete method it names is a reference, so use a better one when you have it, but never lower the outcome or its criteria. Project rules outside this block add to them; a project rule may tighten C1, C3, C8, C9, C11, C12 and C20 but never relax them.

### Sources of truth and loading

- **C1** Every convention has exactly one editable source, so every client reads the same text: `AGENTS.md`, the rules directory (`.agents/rules/`) and the skills directory (`.agents/skills/`). Client entry points such as `CLAUDE.md`, `.claude/rules` and `.claude/skills` are relative symlinks to them; a second copy or a reversed link lets the two drift apart.
- **C2** Each constraint lives at the tier matching its reach, so it is always read when needed and costs no context otherwise: global red lines in this root file, subsystem guards in the rules directory with their scope in `paths` frontmatter, multi-step procedures in skills loaded on demand. Red lines never move down a tier, because lower tiers are not guaranteed to load.
- **C3** Before editing, know which rules govern the files you will touch; before finishing, every rule touched by the actual diff is satisfied. Clients load rules incompletely, so the output of `npx canons scopes <file-or-dir>...` (pass the planned path for new files) and `npx canons scopes --changed` is authoritative. No match does not mean no constraints: this file still applies.
- **C4** Every client must load this file whole, so it stays within its byte budget (`npx canons verify` enforces it). To make room, condense wording or move rationale into docs; never delete a red line.

### Knowledge and documents

- **C5** Conventions an agent must remember are visible to every person and agent and go through review: they live in repository files reviewed through git, never only in a client's private memory. Pitfalls that apply across modules are collected in one lessons file (symptom, cause, how to avoid, invariant), merged by topic so the next reader finds them in one place.
- **C6** Docs and rules give the reader current, correct knowledge and its reasons: no history; facts the code shows directly get a pointer rather than a copy that can drift; invariants that must hold are guarded by tests, not by prose alone; each constraint is written in exactly one place.
- **C7** The repository keeps only what stays useful. Temporary files, one-off scripts and in-flight plans go in the temporary directory (`tmp/` unless C17 says otherwise; git-ignored); reusable tools are committed. Docs and code never point at files there, since they can vanish at any time.

### Collaboration and authority

- **C8** Changes to Git state (commit, push, pull, merge, rebase, reset, stash, tag, switching branches, opening a PR) are the user's call, because they affect shared history, other people's work and releases. Without an explicit instruction from the user, do not make them. Read-only commands and the upstream sync in C9 are fine. Steps of an already authorized task need no second confirmation.
- **C9** Your changes start from the latest upstream code and never overwrite someone else's in-progress work, so nothing is redone on stale code or turned into a needless conflict: before you start, know what is already changed in the working tree (for example with `git status`) and pull the latest upstream (for example `git fetch`, then fast-forward the current branch or start a new branch from the freshly fetched base). Ask the user when syncing would need a merge or rebase or would touch someone else's in-progress changes, and before editing a file another session is changing. Prefer a separate worktree for parallel work; worktrees do not isolate databases, ports or other shared resources.
- **C10** When requirements, behavior, interfaces or naming are genuinely ambiguous, or a user decision conflicts with these rules, the user decides; do not assume. Make the decision quick and informed: name the point of divergence, give mutually exclusive options with your recommendation and its cost (for example 2–4 options, the recommended one first), then wait.
- **C11** Readers can always tell fact from inference: mark unverified judgements as unverified, with their basis and how to verify them; label second-hand conclusions with their source and never promote them to fact.
- **C12** A missing capability (no sub-agents, no browser, no question UI) changes how you work, not what is required: required confirmations and verification still happen, and anything left unverified is reported as such.
- **C13** After a handoff, the receiving agent can continue without coming back to ask. Write the handoff in `tmp/` and pass it on explicitly; it usually needs the goal, scope, changed files, decisions, verification results, remaining work and open decisions. Durable knowledge goes back into docs.
- **C14** At the end of every stage, the user can see at a glance whether this session is done and safe to archive; for anything not done, where it is stuck, who owns it and what happens next (for example as a table: item | status or blocker | owner | next step). Unmerged PRs, pending deploys, pending re-tests and pending user decisions all count as not done.

### Finishing a change

- **C15** When a change lands, code, tests, docs and rules all say the same thing: logic that can be tested automatically has tests, and affected docs and the rules guarding touched invariants are updated in the same change. Report what was updated and, for anything not updated, why not.

### Language and layout

- **C16** Users read the project's UI language and developers read its developer language, so `AGENTS.md` records both outside this block. The UI language covers every user-facing string: buttons, labels, placeholders, empty states, errors, examples, defaults and notifications; when it is not recorded, confirm it with the developer before writing such text and record the answer, never guess. Talk with developers, and write commit messages, pull request descriptions, docs and code comments, in the recorded developer language; when none is recorded, use the system language. Identifiers, paths, commands and technical terms keep their original form.
- **C17** People and agents can predict where things live, following the directory layout recorded in `AGENTS.md`. Without one, the default is: source in `src/`, docs in `doc/`, temporary files in `tmp/` (git-ignored), and every other top-level directory also gets a three-letter name (for example `out/`, `ops/`, `bin/`). The root holds only repository-level configuration and entry files such as `README.md` and `AGENTS.md`.

### Working in the codebase

- **C18** New files and directories read as part of the same set as their neighbours: first the same length (the same number of letters, extension excluded), then the same part of speech, singular or plural, segmentation, case and separators. When neighbours disagree, follow the larger and more recent group; ask when genuinely unsure.
- **C19** After a change to shared semantics (an API parameter, a hook, a constant and the like), every caller and use is still correct, so review every call site before changing it. When a change creates a coupling that must stay in step across several places, record it as a sync point in the docs so the next person changes them together.
- **C20** Whether to change another repository (siblings, reference implementations, dependencies checked out nearby) is the user's call: read freely, change nothing without permission. In a worktree, `../` is not necessarily a sibling repository; confirm the actual path.
- **C21** What the project deliberately defers or declines is the project's call, listed in its docs; do not add it on the side, however useful it looks. When something looks missing, check that list first.

## Project settings

- UI language: English. Every user-facing string the CLI prints and every shipped default is English; rule content ships in English with translations.
- Developer language: English (commit messages, pull requests, docs, code comments).
- Directory layout: `src/` source (code, tests, build script, rule content), `doc/` docs, `out/` build output (git-ignored), `tmp/` temporary files (git-ignored); `.github/` holds GitHub community files and workflows.

## Project rules

- Layout: all source lives in `src/` — code, tests (`src/test/`, fixtures in `src/test/fixtures/`), build script and rule content (`src/canon/`). Only repository-level config (`package.json`, `tsconfig*.json`, `canons.json` and the like) sits at the root. Documentation goes in `doc/`, except `README*.md` and `AGENTS.md`; GitHub community files (`CONTRIBUTING.md`, `SECURITY.md`, `CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md`) go in `.github/` so GitHub still recognizes them. Build output is `out/` (git-ignored).
- Development commands: `npm run typecheck`, `npm test`, `npm run build && node out/cli.js verify`. Run all three before finishing a change.
- In this repository run the CLI from source, `node src/cli.ts <command>`, wherever the canons block says `npx canons` (this repository has no installed copy of the package).
- Releasing: bump `version` in `package.json`, run `node src/cli.ts update --accept-major` so this repository's own block and lock follow, update `doc/CHANGELOG.md`, then tag `v<version>`; `.github/workflows/release.yml` publishes.
- Zero runtime dependencies. Checks stay deterministic: no network, no AI, no clock.
- Shipped content (everything under `src/` except the `*.test.ts` files, plus the READMEs) stays project-neutral; `src/test/locales.test.ts` enforces a deny-list.
- Rule content rules: see `.agents/rules/locale.md` and [CONTRIBUTING.md](.github/CONTRIBUTING.md).
